claim: Invasive species represent one of the foremost risks to global biodiversity.
source: Invasive species represent one of the foremost risks to global biodiversity.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific consensus about invasive species impacts.

claim: The invasion of S. pimpinellifolium onto the Galápagos Islands was recent and largely the result of a single event from central Ecuador.
source: Using >300 archipelago and mainland collections, we infer this invasion was recent and largely the result of a single event from central Ecuador.
evidence: This claim is supported by population genomic analyses presented in the manuscript, including demographic reconstruction and geographic origin inference.

claim: Post-colonization hybridization and introgression occurred between S. pimpinellifolium and S. cheesmaniae.
source: Patterns of ancestry within the genomes of invasive plants also reveal post-colonization hybridization and introgression between S. pimpinellifolium and the closely related Galápagos endemic Solanum cheesmaniae.
evidence: This is supported by genomic ancestry analyses including fastStructure, NewHybrids, Treemix, and HMM-based local ancestry inference.

claim: Admixed invasive individuals carrying endemic alleles at carotenoid biosynthesis loci have orange fruits instead of typical red S. pimpinellifolium fruits.
source: Of admixed invasive individuals, those that carry endemic alleles at one of two different carotenoid biosynthesis loci also have orange fruits—characteristic of the endemic species—instead of typical red S. pimpinellifolium fruits.
evidence: This is supported by admixture mapping showing association between local ancestry at carotenoid loci and fruit color phenotypes.

claim: Introgression of two independent fruit color loci explains the observed trait convergence to orange fruits.
source: We infer that introgression of two independent fruit color loci explains this observed trait convergence, suggesting that selection has favored repeated transitions of red to orange fruits on the Galápagos.
evidence: This is based on the association between CHS ancestry at PSY1 (chromosome 3) in MG114 and CYC-B (chromosome 6) in MG117 with orange fruit phenotypes.

claim: Selection has favored repeated transitions of red to orange fruits on the Galápagos.
source: We infer that introgression of two independent fruit color loci explains this observed trait convergence, suggesting that selection has favored repeated transitions of red to orange fruits on the Galápagos.
evidence: This is inferred from the repeated independent introgression of different carotenoid loci associated with orange fruit color.

claim: Introduction events are often associated with strong genetic bottlenecks.
source: Introduction events are often associated with strong genetic bottlenecks (Kolbe et al., 2004; Colautti et al., 2005; Golani et al., 2007) and reduced effective population sizes, features which may constrain the ability of colonizers to adapt to novel environments and compete with native biota (Lande, 1988; Lee, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Genetic bottlenecks may constrain the ability of colonizers to adapt to novel environments and compete with native biota.
source: Introduction events are often associated with strong genetic bottlenecks (Kolbe et al., 2004; Colautti et al., 2005; Golani et al., 2007) and reduced effective population sizes, features which may constrain the ability of colonizers to adapt to novel environments and compete with native biota (Lande, 1988; Lee, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: Diversity could be maintained by multiple independent introductions.
source: Despite intense bottlenecks, diversity could be maintained by other means, including multiple independent introductions (Facon et al., 2008; Kolbe et al., 2004) or via hybridization with congenerics present in the new habitat (Ellstrand and Schierenbeck, 2000; Lavergne and Molofsky, 2007; Reatini and Vision, 2020; Stepien et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Diversity could be maintained via hybridization with congenerics present in the new habitat.
source: Despite intense bottlenecks, diversity could be maintained by other means, including multiple independent introductions (Facon et al., 2008; Kolbe et al., 2004) or via hybridization with congenerics present in the new habitat (Ellstrand and Schierenbeck, 2000; Lavergne and Molofsky, 2007; Reatini and Vision, 2020; Stepien et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hybridization might be particularly important for facilitating invasion into island habitats.
source: Of these mechanisms, hybridization might be particularly important for facilitating invasion into island habitats.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the unique characteristics of island environments discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Hybridization among native and introduced taxa is common on islands.
source: Hybridization among native and introduced taxa is common on islands (Carlquist, 1974), potentially because of limitations on geographic extent, the abundance of generalist pollinators (Olesen et al., 2002), and/or frequent anthropogenic disturbance (Bertolo et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013; Long et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two yellow/orange-fruited tomato species are considered endemic to the Galápagos Islands: Solanum cheesmaniae and Solanum galapagense.
source: Two yellow/orange-fruited tomato species are considered endemic to the islands: Solanum cheesmaniae (L. Riley) Fosberg [CHS] and Solanum galapagense S.C. Darwin and Peralta [GAL] (Appendix 1, section S1).
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge about Galápagos tomato species.

claim: Two red-fruited invasive species from continental Ecuador and Peru are now documented on the Galápagos archipelago: Solanum pimpinellifolium and Solanum lycopersicum.
source: Two red-fruited invasive species from continental Ecuador and Peru are now also documented on the archipelago: Solanum pimpinellifolium L. [PIM] and Solanum lycopersicum L. [LYC]—the domesticated tomato.
evidence: This is based on field observations and previous documentation.

claim: Domesticated S. lycopersicum was almost certainly introduced for agriculture.
source: Domesticated LYC was almost certainly introduced for agriculture (Rick, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and logical inference about domesticated crop introduction.

claim: Wild species S. pimpinellifolium was likely introduced by early human colonizers.
source: Wild species PIM was also likely introduced by early human colonizers (Darwin et al., 2003; Darwin, 2009), however the timing and source of this introduction is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous hypotheses, though the timing and source were unknown prior to this study.

claim: Recent field surveys indicate substantially increased abundance of the invasive species while abundance of the two endemic species has markedly declined over the past two decades.
source: Recent field surveys indicate substantially increased abundance of the invasive species while abundance of the two endemic species has markedly declined over the past two decades (Darwin, 2009; Nuez et al., 2004; Gibson et al., 2020), suggesting that recent demographic shifts may pose an extinction threat to the endemic species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to field survey data.

claim: Recent demographic shifts may pose an extinction threat to the endemic species.
source: Recent field surveys indicate substantially increased abundance of the invasive species while abundance of the two endemic species has markedly declined over the past two decades (Darwin, 2009; Nuez et al., 2004; Gibson et al., 2020), suggesting that recent demographic shifts may pose an extinction threat to the endemic species.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed demographic trends.

claim: There is high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species due to overlapping habitats.
source: Several factors also indicate a high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species, including overlapping habitats (Darwin, 2009; Nuez et al., 2004), similar flower morphologies (Darwin et al., 2003; Darwin, 2009; Rick et al., 1977; Vosters et al., 2014), and shared pollinators (Darwin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous observations.

claim: There is high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species due to similar flower morphologies.
source: Several factors also indicate a high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species, including overlapping habitats (Darwin, 2009; Nuez et al., 2004), similar flower morphologies (Darwin et al., 2003; Darwin, 2009; Rick et al., 1977; Vosters et al., 2014), and shared pollinators (Darwin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous observations.

claim: There is high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species due to shared pollinators.
source: Several factors also indicate a high potential for hybridization between native and invasive species, including overlapping habitats (Darwin, 2009; Nuez et al., 2004), similar flower morphologies (Darwin et al., 2003; Darwin, 2009; Rick et al., 1977; Vosters et al., 2014), and shared pollinators (Darwin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous observations.

claim: All four tomato species are closely related, having diverged less than 500 kya.
source: Moreover, all four species are closely related—having diverged less than 500 kya (Pease et al., 2016)—and all can be crossed to produce hybrids in the greenhouse (Rick, 1956; Rick and Bowman, 1961; Rick and Fobes, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a phylogenetic study.

claim: All four tomato species can be crossed to produce hybrids in the greenhouse.
source: Moreover, all four species are closely related—having diverged less than 500 kya (Pease et al., 2016)—and all can be crossed to produce hybrids in the greenhouse (Rick, 1956; Rick and Bowman, 1961; Rick and Fobes, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental crossing studies.

claim: The study used genomic sequencing data from 174 plants representing all four species from the largest islands of San Cristobal, Santa Cruz, and Isabela.
source: Using genomic sequencing data from 174 plants (representing all four species) from the largest islands of San Cristobal, Santa Cruz, and Isabela, and a panel of 132 mainland PIM accessions from across the entire native range on continental South America, we (i) infer the timing, source, and number of invasions by PIM onto the Galápagos and (ii) evaluate evidence for post-colonization gene flow between the four tomato taxa, and its evolutionary consequences.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The study used a panel of 132 mainland PIM accessions from across the entire native range on continental South America.
source: Using genomic sequencing data from 174 plants (representing all four species) from the largest islands of San Cristobal, Santa Cruz, and Isabela, and a panel of 132 mainland PIM accessions from across the entire native range on continental South America, we (i) infer the timing, source, and number of invasions by PIM onto the Galápagos and (ii) evaluate evidence for post-colonization gene flow between the four tomato taxa, and its evolutionary consequences.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The majority of PIM originated in central Ecuador.
source: We find that the majority of PIM originated in central Ecuador, are the product of a recent invasion, and are actively hybridizing with an endemic relative.
evidence: This is based on population genetic analyses including Locator predictions and divergence patterns.

claim: Invasive PIM are the product of a recent invasion.
source: We find that the majority of PIM originated in central Ecuador, are the product of a recent invasion, and are actively hybridizing with an endemic relative.
evidence: This is based on demographic reconstruction using δaδi.

claim: Invasive PIM are actively hybridizing with an endemic relative.
source: We find that the majority of PIM originated in central Ecuador, are the product of a recent invasion, and are actively hybridizing with an endemic relative.
evidence: This is based on genomic ancestry analyses showing recent and ongoing gene flow.

claim: The emergence of novel orange-fruited plants in two invasive populations can be explained by endemic introgression at distinct carotenoid loci.
source: By characterizing fine-scale local ancestry, we find that the emergence of novel orange-fruited plants—which resemble the endemic species in color—in two invasive populations can be explained by endemic introgression at distinct carotenoid loci with known phenotypic effects specifically on fruit color.
evidence: This is based on admixture mapping showing association between local ancestry at CYC-B and PSY1 with fruit color.

claim: The introgressed carotenoid loci have known phenotypic effects specifically on fruit color.
source: By characterizing fine-scale local ancestry, we find that the emergence of novel orange-fruited plants—which resemble the endemic species in color—in two invasive populations can be explained by endemic introgression at distinct carotenoid loci with known phenotypic effects specifically on fruit color.
evidence: This is based on previous functional studies of CYC-B and PSY1 cited in the manuscript.

claim: Sequence data were drawn from 306 individual samples.
source: Sequence data were drawn from 306 individual samples.
evidence: This describes the sample size of the study.

claim: Double-digest RAD sequencing was performed using PstI and EcoRI enzymes.
source: We performed double-digest RAD (ddRAD) sequencing (using PstI and EcoRI enzymes) of 174 wild collected individuals from 13 populations of endemic and invasive tomatoes from three islands in the Galápagos archipelago: San Cristobal, Santa Cruz, and Isabela (Figure 1; Table 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology.

claim: 18,573 high-quality RAD loci were recovered, each sequenced to an average of 61.4× in 80% of all 306 samples.
source: We recovered 18,573 high-quality RAD loci, each sequenced to an average of 61.4× (s.d. = 35×) in 80% of all 306 samples (Supplementary file 1c and 1d).
evidence: This describes the sequencing results.

claim: Average insert size was 192 bp after adapter and quality trimming.
source: Average insert size was 192 bp (s.d. = 51.7) after adapter and quality trimming.
evidence: This describes the sequencing results.

claim: After filtering for depth (>8 reads), 11,297 SNPs were retained.
source: After filtering for depth (>8 reads), 11,297 SNPs were retained.
evidence: This describes the data filtering process.

claim: After filtering for LD (r2 < 0.7), 5767 SNPs were retained.
source: After filtering for LD (r2 < 0.7), 5767 SNPs were retained.
evidence: This describes the data filtering process.

claim: Approximately 40% of individuals in populations MG114 and MG117 have orange instead of red fruits.
source: Inset: Photograph of polymorphic (red/orange) PIM fruits representative of populations MG114 and MG117.
evidence: This is based on field observations and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Nucleotide diversity was reduced on average 6.6-fold in island populations relative to mainland accessions.
source: Nucleotide diversity (π in 100 kb overlapping windows; Figure 2C) was reduced on average 6.6-fold in island populations relative to mainland accessions (Table 1), a pattern consistent with population genetic expectations following colonization.
evidence: This is based on calculations of nucleotide diversity from the genomic data.

claim: The reduction in nucleotide diversity in island populations is consistent with population genetic expectations following colonization.
source: Nucleotide diversity (π in 100 kb overlapping windows; Figure 2C) was reduced on average 6.6-fold in island populations relative to mainland accessions (Table 1), a pattern consistent with population genetic expectations following colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on population genetic theory.

claim: Genetic variation in the native (mainland) range of PIM is highly geographically structured.
source: Genetic variation in the native (mainland) range of PIM is highly geographically structured (Gibson and Moyle, 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), allowing us to infer a putative origin of PIM lineages invasive on the Galápagos.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A rate-smoothed maximum likelihood tree identified Galápagos PIM as monophyletic.
source: A rate-smoothed maximum likelihood tree constructed in Treemix (Pickrell and Pritchard, 2012) identified Galápagos PIM as monophyletic, and clearly separated island and non-island clades (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pairwise sequence divergence was lower in Galápagos-Ecuador comparisons than between Galápagos-Peru comparisons.
source: In general, pairwise sequence divergence was lower in Galápagos-Ecuador comparisons (average dxy = 2.3×103) than between Galápagos-Peru comparisons (average dxy = 3.6×103; Figure 2C), and samples showing low genome-wide divergence were clustered in central Ecuador (similar patterns were observed using FST; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is based on calculations of pairwise divergence from the genomic data.

claim: Locator predictions indicated two to three source regions for Galápagos PIM.
source: Locator predictions indicated two to three source regions for Galápagos PIM, although the exact locations varied across runs and depended on which island PIM collections were considered (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on machine learning predictions using the Locator software.

claim: Santa Cruz and San Cristobal PIM collections were predicted to have originated in central Ecuador.
source: Santa Cruz and San Cristobal PIM collections were predicted to have originated in central Ecuador; this result was generally consistent across runs, with the consensus being an origin near Los Rios and Guayas provinces in southcentral Ecuador (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on Locator predictions.

claim: One mainland accession (LA0411) represents a back migration from the Galápagos to Los Rios.
source: Interestingly, we also infer that one mainland accession represents a back migration from the Galápagos to Los Rios (LA0411; Appendix 1, section S2), further highlighting the high degree of connectivity between this region and the islands.
evidence: This is based on Locator predictions and phylogenetic placement.

claim: LA3123 was predicted to have originated in Peru.
source: In contrast, the remaining two samples, LA3123 (a historical collection from Santa Cruz sampled in 1991) and MG128-1 (newly sampled on Isabela), were predicted to have originated in alternative locations, with most runs supporting a Peruvian origin for LA3123 and an Ecuadorian origin for MG128-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on Locator predictions.

claim: MG128-1 was predicted to have originated in Ecuador.
source: In contrast, the remaining two samples, LA3123 (a historical collection from Santa Cruz sampled in 1991) and MG128-1 (newly sampled on Isabela), were predicted to have originated in alternative locations, with most runs supporting a Peruvian origin for LA3123 and an Ecuadorian origin for MG128-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on Locator predictions.

claim: The data support two to three independent introductions of PIM onto the archipelago.
source: Together our data support two to three independent introductions of PIM onto the archipelago, each with variable consequences for current invasive populations: (i) a minor event from Peru [LA3123], (ii) a minor event from Ecuador [MG128-1], and (iii) a major event from central Ecuador that is responsible for nearly all sampled populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of genomic evidence.

claim: A major introduction event from central Ecuador is responsible for nearly all sampled populations.
source: Together our data support two to three independent introductions of PIM onto the archipelago, each with variable consequences for current invasive populations: (i) a minor event from Peru [LA3123], (ii) a minor event from Ecuador [MG128-1], and (iii) a major event from central Ecuador that is responsible for nearly all sampled populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of genomic evidence.

claim: The two-epoch instantaneous size change model fit the data better than a neutral model of constant population size.
source: The two-epoch model thus included five parameters: epoch one population size (NB), epoch two population size (NF), timing of the first size change (TB), timing of second size change (TF), and the inbreeding coefficient. To limit potential confounding effects due to population structure within PIM, we estimated the folded site frequency spectrum (SFS) of a single population (MG114, which was the most deeply sampled of our PIM populations). We also masked regions of inferred introgression (as detected by our hidden Markov model [HMM], see below) as these can spuriously inflate rare variants and thus bias the inference of a bottleneck and subsequent parameter estimation (Appendix 1, section S3). In our masked dataset, we observed a large excess of rare variants (genome-wide Tajima's D = −0.49 ±0.12; Figure 2—figure supplement 5) more consistent with a bottleneck model (RSSBottle = 0.23; ln(L)=−18.46) than a neutral model (RSSNeutral = 16.61; ln(L)=−26.63).
evidence: This is based on model comparison using δaδi.

claim: A recent bottleneck occurred 201.66 generations in the past.
source: We used the best-fit bottleneck model to estimate the timing of the introduction by performing a two-step optimization procedure. We inferred a recent bottleneck occurring 201.66 (TB +TF) generations in the past (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on demographic inference using δaδi.

claim: The bootstrapped median estimate for the time to bottleneck was 200.17 generations.
source: Bootstrapped CIs for TB and TF were relatively small (2–493 gen for TB; 30–401 gen for TF), and medians were in close agreement with optimized estimates (Table 2). The bootstrapped median estimate for the time to bottleneck was 200.17, which is less than two generations away from the optimized estimate.
evidence: This is based on bootstrap analysis of the demographic model.

claim: The inferred expansion in CHS is nearly eight times older than the bottleneck in PIM.
source: For comparison, we also model the history of an endemic CHS population (MG115) using the same framework as above. The two-epoch model again fit the data better (ln(L)=−44.61) than a neutral model (ln(L)=−74.18). In addition, we infer a large expansion phase occurring between 1114 and 1845 generations ago followed by a very recent and strong contraction (Supplementary file 1g). Compared to our estimate of the timing of the bottleneck in PIM, the inferred expansion in CHS is nearly eight times older.
evidence: This is based on demographic inference for CHS population MG115.

claim: Tajima's D was higher in MG115 (D = −0.18 ± 0.08) compared to invasive PIM MG114.
source: Tajima's D was also higher in MG115 (D = −0.18 ± 0.08) compared to invasive PIM MG114, which is more consistent with neutral expectations and a larger fraction of intermediate frequency alleles.
evidence: This is based on calculations of Tajima's D from the genomic data.

claim: The close evolutionary relationship of PIM, CHS, and GAL indicates the potential for interspecific gene flow may be high.
source: The close evolutionary relationship of PIM, CHS, and GAL, their similar floral morphologies, and the presence of only a single major pollinator on the islands (Xylocarpii darwini; McMullen, 1999), indicate the potential for interspecific gene flow between tomato species may be high.
evidence: This is an inference based on biological characteristics and a citation.

claim: There is only a single major pollinator on the islands (Xylocarpii darwini).
source: The close evolutionary relationship of PIM, CHS, and GAL, their similar floral morphologies, and the presence of only a single major pollinator on the islands (Xylocarpii darwini; McMullen, 1999), indicate the potential for interspecific gene flow between tomato species may be high.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: A novel fruit color polymorphism exists in two Santa Cruz PIM populations (MG114 and MG117).
source: In particular, we have previously described a novel fruit color polymorphism in two Santa Cruz PIM populations (MG114 and MG117; Gibson et al., 2020), where approximately 40% of individuals have orange instead of their ancestrally red fruits.
evidence: This is based on field observations reported in a previous publication.

claim: Orange fruits are very rare in mainland PIM.
source: Orange fruits are very rare in mainland PIM (TGRC passport data; http://www.tgrc.ucdavis.edu) but are diagnostic of the two endemic Galápagos species.
evidence: This is based on data from the Tomato Genetics Resource Center.

claim: Orange fruits are diagnostic of the two endemic Galápagos species.
source: Orange fruits are very rare in mainland PIM (TGRC passport data; http://www.tgrc.ucdavis.edu) but are diagnostic of the two endemic Galápagos species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the endemic species.

claim: No evidence of early generation CHS×PIM hybrids was found in polymorphic PIM populations MG114 and MG117.
source: Interestingly, we find no evidence of early generation CHS×PIM hybrids in either of the polymorphic PIM populations MG114 and MG117 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on fastStructure and NewHybrids analyses.

claim: Variable levels of CHS×PIM admixture were detected at site MG115.
source: However, these analyses did detect variable levels of CHS×PIM admixture at the nearby site MG115 (Figure 3A), a pattern which is also reflected in principal component space (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on fastStructure and PCA analyses.

claim: 4/6 of admixed plants at MG115 were classified as first- or second-generation hybrids.
source: Using NewHybrids, we classified 4/6 of these admixed plants as first- or second-generation hybrids (Supplementary file 1h, i and j).
evidence: This is based on NewHybrids analysis.

claim: Treemix analysis implies three separate admixture events between PIM and CHS.
source: To complement the above analyses, we employed Treemix (Pickrell and Pritchard, 2012). The most likely topology inferred by Treemix implies three separate admixture events between PIM and CHS: two cases of CHS → PIM admixture and one case of PIM → CHS admixture on Santa Cruz (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: This is based on Treemix analysis.

claim: The D-statistic was 0.818 (s.d. = 0.028; bootstrapped p<0.02), indicating strong evidence for admixture between island PIM and CHS.
source: As independent support for a history of gene flow, we calculated the four taxa D-statistic of Durand et al., 2011 using Solanum pennellii (LA3778) as an outgroup and treating PIM population MG114 and CHS (MG115) as P2 and P3, respectively. We found that D was 0.818 (s.d. = 0.028; bootstrapped p<0.02), indicating an excess of ABBA sites and strong evidence for admixture between island PIM and CHS.
evidence: This is based on D-statistic calculation.

claim: D was also significant when other invasive PIM populations were used as P2.
source: D was also significant when other invasive PIM populations—Santa Cruz population MG117 or San Cristobal populations MG107 and MG105—were used as P2, indicating that the detected admixture likely predates the dispersal and differentiation between Santa Cruz and San Cristobal invasive PIM.
evidence: This is based on D-statistic calculations for multiple populations.

claim: The HMM detected clear evidence for CHS ancestry within the polymorphic PIM populations MG114 and MG117.
source: Our HMM detected clear evidence for CHS ancestry within the polymorphic PIM populations MG114 and MG117, reflecting admixture from CHS → PIM.
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: Inferred admixture in nonpolymorphic PIM (e.g., MG116) was much more restricted.
source: In contrast, inferred admixture in nonpolymorphic PIM (e.g., MG116) was much more restricted.
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: For MG114, CHS ancestry blocks composed on average 3.64% of the genomes of any given MG114 plant.
source: For MG114, CHS ancestry blocks were large (average = 16,235 kb), of varying size (sd = 139.43 kb), and composed on average 3.64% of the genomes of any given MG114 plant (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: Shared ancestry between MG114 and MG115 was dominated by two large CHS haplotypes segregating at moderate to high frequencies on chromosome three (40%) and chromosome six (20%).
source: Shared ancestry between MG114 and MG115 was dominated by two large CHS haplotypes segregating at moderate to high frequencies on chromosome three (40%; mean size = 51.35 Mb) and chromosome six (20%; mean size = 35.3 Mb; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: In MG117, CHS ancestry made up 4.36% of any given MG117 genome.
source: In MG117, CHS ancestry made up 4.36% (sd = 2.56%) of any given MG117 genome and average block size was 9,687.5 kb (Figure 4C,D; Supplementary file 1m).
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: A large CHS haplotype on chromosome six occurs at a frequency of 0.42 in MG117.
source: As with MG114, a large CHS haplotype on chromosome six occurs at a frequency of 0.42.
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: In MG116, CHS ancestry blocks made up a substantially smaller fraction of the total genome (average admixture proportion = 0.55%).
source: In comparison to MG114 and MG117, MG116 showed little evidence for shared ancestry. While 3/7 individuals had inferred signals of CHS ancestry, these blocks were generally small compared to MG114 and MG117 (average = 4,450 kb; Figure 5) and made up a substantially smaller fraction of the total genome (average admixture proportion = 0.55%; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on HMM local ancestry inference.

claim: Age estimates for CHS haplotypes in MG114 and MG117 are within the range of 4–12 generations.
source: In MG114 and MG117, age estimates are within the range of 4–12 generations (e.g., the large chromosome 3 and 6 CHS haplotypes in MG114 are estimated at 4.23 and 4.74 generations, respectively).
evidence: This is based on calculations using block size and recombination rate.

claim: There is close agreement between age estimates in MG114 and MG117, suggesting these instances of CHS introgression might have been derived from the same admixture event.
source: In addition to placing boundaries on when the initial hybridization took place in the past (>4 and up to 12 generations), there is close agreement between age estimates in MG114 and MG117, suggesting that these instances of CHS introgression might have been derived from the same admixture event (Appendix 1, section S4).
evidence: This is an inference based on similar age estimates.

claim: A recent history of hybridization between CHS and GAL was uncovered on Isabela at la Laguna de Manzanilla.
source: In addition to inferred introgression between PIM and CHS, we also found evidence for hybridization/introgression involving the other two taxa: GAL and LYC. In particular, we uncovered a recent history of hybridization between CHS and GAL on Isabela—at la Laguna de Manzanilla (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is based on fastStructure and PCA analyses.

claim: Nine samples at the CHS/GAL site were identified as admixed.
source: Our fastStructure and principal components analyses (PCA) of individuals at this site clearly identify nine samples as admixed (Figure 3B), mostly corresponding with morphological classifications of intermediacy (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on fastStructure and PCA analyses.

claim: Of the nine admixed plants at the CHS/GAL site, four appear to be first generation backcrosses, whereas four are F2.
source: Of the nine admixed plants, four appear to be first generation backcrosses, whereas four are F2 (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is based on NewHybrids analysis.

claim: Putative cases of CHS/GAL×LYC admixture were identified in two populations on Isabela.
source: We also identified putative cases of CHS/GAL×LYC admixture in two populations on Isabela (Figure 3B), although some of these signals might be the product of unmodeled genetic substructure (Appendix 1, section S5).
evidence: This is based on fastStructure analysis, though with some uncertainty.

claim: Low levels of LYC ancestry were detected within some PIM populations on Santa Cruz.
source: On Santa Cruz, low levels of LYC (domesticated tomato) ancestry were also detected within some PIM populations, including a potential hybrid PIM×LYC population MG118 that was predicted to be entirely first-generation hybrids.
evidence: This is based on fastStructure and NewHybrids analyses.

claim: The presence of orange fruits in MG117 correlated perfectly with CHS ancestry at CYC-B on chromosome 6.
source: For MG117, we found that the presence of orange fruits correlated perfectly with CHS ancestry at one carotenoid synthesis gene: CYC-B on chromosome 6 (Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1o). This association is significant based on a χ2 test of independence (χ2 = 8.33; df = 1; p=0.0039).
evidence: This is based on admixture mapping and statistical testing.

claim: CYC-B is a lycopene beta cyclase and the specific locus known to underlie the lighter colored fruits observed in the endemic species.
source: CYC-B is a lycopene beta cyclase and the specific locus known to underlie the lighter (orange) colored fruits observed in the endemic species (Stommel and Haynes, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous functional work.

claim: In MG114, the presence of orange fruits was solely predicted by CHS ancestry at PSY1 on chromosome 3.
source: In contrast, the similarly sized chromosome six haplotype in MG114 (Figure 4B) does not include the CHS allele at the CYC-B locus. Instead, in MG114 we find that the presence of orange fruits was solely predicted by CHS ancestry at PSY1 on chromosome 3, the first enzyme in the carotenoid fruit color pathway (Supplementary file 1p; χ2 = 11.12; df = 1; p=0.0009).
evidence: This is based on admixture mapping and statistical testing.

claim: Loss of function mutations in PSY1 have been described in LYC and these produce orange fruit color.
source: Although the role of PSY1 in the coloration of endemic fruits has not yet been studied, loss of function mutations in PSY1 have been described in LYC and these produce orange fruit color (Fray and Grierson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous functional work.

claim: PSY1 is expressed at detectable levels in both endemic species.
source: To further investigate the association of PSY1 with endemic fruit pigmentation, we used previously published RNAseq data (Pease et al., 2016) to examine variation in PSY1 across the entire wild tomato clade. PSY1 is expressed at detectable levels in both endemic species and has a highly conserved coding sequence (1203/1239 shared sites), whose exceptions include a single non-synonymous substitution (62R → W) unique to the endemic clade (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published RNAseq data.

claim: PSY1 has a highly conserved coding sequence (1203/1239 shared sites) across the wild tomato clade.
source: PSY1 is expressed at detectable levels in both endemic species and has a highly conserved coding sequence (1203/1239 shared sites), whose exceptions include a single non-synonymous substitution (62R → W) unique to the endemic clade (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published RNAseq data.

claim: A single non-synonymous substitution (62R → W) in PSY1 is unique to the endemic clade.
source: PSY1 is expressed at detectable levels in both endemic species and has a highly conserved coding sequence (1203/1239 shared sites), whose exceptions include a single non-synonymous substitution (62R → W) unique to the endemic clade (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published RNAseq data.

claim: The 62R → W substitution in PSY1 lies outside of the trans-isoprenyl diphosphate synthase protein domain but within the transit peptide signal sequence.
source: This substitution lies outside of the trans-isoprenyl diphosphate synthase protein domain associated with the enzyme's function, but within the transit peptide signal sequence (residues 1–70), although the specific functional importance of this variant remains to be assessed.
evidence: This is based on protein domain analysis.

claim: Two separate mechanisms underlie the emergence of orange fruits in Galápagos PIM, both likely derived via introgression from CHS.
source: Regardless, based on our observed associations between carotenoid biosynthesis loci and fruit color variation, our data support two separate mechanisms underlying the emergence of orange fruits in Galápagos PIM, both of which were likely derived via introgression from CHS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the admixture mapping results.

claim: Invasive populations of S. pimpinellifolium had low levels of genetic diversity and an excess of rare alleles.
source: Invasive populations of S. pimpinellifolium (PIM) had low levels of genetic diversity and an excess of rare alleles, and we inferred two to three recent introductions onto the archipelago from Ecuador and Peru.
evidence: This is based on nucleotide diversity calculations and Tajima's D.

claim: Only a single introduction event from Ecuador comprises 98% of sampled invasives on the archipelago.
source: Our analyses identify three independent introduction events, yet only a single event from Ecuador comprises 98% of sampled invasives on the archipelago.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and population genetic analyses.

claim: The consensus prediction supports a southcentral origin near Guayas or Los Rios provinces for the primary introduction.
source: For the primary introduction, although we observed variance in source region predictions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the consensus prediction supports a southcentral origin near Guayas or Los Rios provinces.
evidence: This is based on Locator predictions and divergence patterns.

claim: One of the earliest and largest bursts of human migration to Galápagos coincided with the Tungurahua province earthquake in 1949.
source: First, although Ecuadorian colonizers of the Galápagos originate from across the country, one of the earliest and largest bursts of migration coincided with the Tungurahua province earthquake in 1949 (Toral-Granda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to historical records.

claim: The vast majority of all trade between Galápagos and the continent occurred from Guayaquil.
source: Second, the vast majority of all trade between Galápagos and the continent occurred—and continues to occur—from Guayaquil, the second largest city in Ecuador (Lundh, 2004; Toral-Granda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical records.

claim: PIM is most likely the result of a recent, human-mediated expansion on the archipelago.
source: We conclude that PIM is most likely the result of a recent, human-mediated expansion on the archipelago.
evidence: This is an inference based on demographic reconstruction and historical context.

claim: Human introduced species represent upward of 70% of all alien plant species on the Galápagos.
source: Human introduced species represent upward of 70% of all alien plant species on the Galápagos (Quiroga, 2018), and PIM has similarly been hypothesized to be the product of a human introduction; however the timing and mode of its introduction—including the role of humans—was not previously known.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Hybridization could help overcome the adaptive limits imposed by genetic bottlenecks during colonization.
source: Hybridization has been hypothesized as a mechanism for promoting invasive colonization success, as it could help overcome the adaptive limits that might otherwise be imposed by genetic bottlenecks during the colonization process (the so-called 'genetic paradox' of invasion; Allendorf and Lundquist, 2003; Sakai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The most prominent signal of gene flow is between PIM and CHS.
source: The most prominent signal of gene flow is between PIM and CHS (Figure 3; Figure 4; Figure 5), including clear evidence for both early generation (F1 and F2) hybrid offspring and older introgression 4–12 generations in the past.
evidence: This is based on multiple genomic analyses.

claim: Gene flow between PIM and CHS is ongoing.
source: Our results indicate (i) that CHS ancestry is maintained in some PIM populations beyond initial hybridization and (ii) that gene flow is ongoing.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of both early and later generation hybrids.

claim: The persistence of later generation CHS×PIM hybrids indicates they are not immediately selected against.
source: While we do not have direct data on relative fitness of hybrids, the persistence of later generation CHS×PIM hybrids indicates they are not immediately selected against.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of later generation hybrids.

claim: The genomes of most admixed PIM are consistent with a history of secondary contact characterized not by strong hybrid incompatibility, but a less restricted exchange of alleles.
source: Indeed, the genomes of most admixed PIM (MG114 and MG117) are consistent with a history of secondary contact and gene flow characterized not by strong hybrid incompatibility, but a less restricted exchange of alleles between species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic patterns of introgression.

claim: The nonrandom distribution of CHS ancestry throughout admixed PIM suggests it may be selectively maintained in certain regions of the genome.
source: Furthermore, the nonrandom distribution of CHS ancestry throughout admixed PIM suggests that it may be selectively maintained in certain regions of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of CHS ancestry on specific chromosomes.

claim: Introgression is likely the source of phenotypic convergence on orange fruits observed in invasive Santa Cruz PIM.
source: A key finding of our analyses is that introgression is likely the source of phenotypic convergence on orange fruits that is observed in invasive Santa Cruz PIM.
evidence: This is based on admixture mapping showing association between introgressed loci and fruit color.

claim: Orange/yellow fruit color is diagnostic for the endemic species.
source: Orange/yellow fruit color is diagnostic for the endemic species (CHS is typically pale yellow; GAL is typically orange) but extremely rare in PIM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species.

claim: The very few described examples of orange fruits among continental PIM are all located in Peru.
source: The very few described examples of orange fruits among continental PIM are all located in Peru (e.g., Sifres et al., 2007), and none have been reported in the inferred geographic region of origin of this invasion (TGRC passport data; http://www.tgrc.ucdavis.edu).
evidence: This is based on TGRC database records and a citation.

claim: CYC-B mutants were first identified as natural allelic variation in the endemic species CHS.
source: Interestingly, CYC-B mutants were first identified as natural allelic variation in the endemic species CHS (Rick, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Introgression of the CHS beta allele at CYC-B into LYC causes the accumulation of β-carotene in ripening tissues and the production of orange fruits.
source: Introgression of the CHS beta allele at CYC-B into LYC causes the accumulation of β-carotene in ripening tissues and the production of orange fruits (Stommel and Haynes, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Orange fruits segregate as a single dominant gene at CYC-B.
source: Orange fruits segregate as a single dominant gene, and genotypic variation at this locus explains a large fraction of fruit color variation in experimental crosses (Rick, 1956; Stommel and Haynes, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Introgression of CHS CYC-B into PIM has the same large, dominant effect on fruit color in admixed individuals.
source: Our data show a clear association between CHS ancestry and orange fruit color at this locus (Figure 5)—including the observation that individuals heterozygous for ancestry display the dominant phenotype—so we infer that introgression of CHS CYC-B into PIM has the same large, dominant effect on fruit color in admixed individuals of this wild species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed association and known genetics of CYC-B.

claim: PSY1 was first identified in the spontaneous fruit color mutant yellow-flesh in LYC.
source: Unlike CYC-B, PSY1 was first identified in the spontaneous fruit color mutant yellow-flesh in LYC (accession LA2997; Fray and Grierson, 1993), and its role has not been directly evaluated in CHS or GAL.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Recessive r mutants at yellow-flesh carry a truncated version of PSY1 that is unable to convert precursor into phytoene.
source: Recessive r mutants at yellow-flesh carry a truncated version of PSY1 that is unable to convert precursor into phytoene. The resulting fruits accumulate almost no carotenoids and the yellow skin pigmentation is driven primarily by the accumulation of the flavonoid chaloconaringenin (Fray and Grierson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous functional work.

claim: No truncation or premature stop mutations were detected in PSY1 in the endemic species.
source: Using previously published RNA-seq data (Pease et al., 2016), we confirmed the expression of PSY1 in both endemic species and did not detect any truncation or premature stop mutations.
evidence: This is based on analysis of previously published RNAseq data.

claim: Disruption of the transit signal sequence may prevent localization to the chloroplast and result in a nonfunctional enzyme.
source: Disruption of the transit signal sequence may prevent localization to the chloroplast and thus result in a nonfunctional enzyme, although determining the exact role PSY1 has in endemic—and by extension PIM—fruit coloration would require future functional confirmation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on protein function knowledge.

claim: CYC-B and PSY1 in invasive orange-fruited PIM are unequivocally derived from CHS.
source: Regardless, CYC-B and PSY1 in invasive orange-fruited PIM are unequivocally derived from CHS, and current functional knowledge of both loci indicate their effects on fruit color could entirely explain observed phenotypic variation in orange-fruited PIM.
evidence: This is based on the admixture mapping results and functional knowledge.

claim: The ubiquitous lighter fruits of the two endemic species and the appearance of convergence toward endemic-like fruit colors in invasive PIM suggest lighter fruits may have a specific selective advantage on the islands.
source: Finally, the ubiquitous lighter (orange and yellow) fruits of the two endemic species, the appearance of convergence toward endemic-like fruit colors in invasive PIM, and the likely independent recruitment of endemic fruit color alleles at PSY1 and CYC-B in MG114 and MG117, together suggest intriguing evidence that lighter fruits may have a specific selective advantage on the islands.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed patterns of introgression and convergence.

claim: Differences in fruit dispersal could be a likely mechanism for selection on fruit color.
source: The potential environmental basis of this selection is unknown, however differences in fruit dispersal—including disperser color preference(s) and/or fruit color apparency—on the islands versus the continental mainland could be a likely mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation about potential selective mechanisms.

claim: Orange pigmentation could arise due to relaxed selection if it is more costly to produce red fruits and they have no specific advantage in island environments.
source: Alternatively, at least in the case of PSY1 which likely involves either a full or partial loss of function, orange pigmentation could arise due to relaxed selection, if it is more costly to produce red fruits and they have no specific advantage in island environments.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative selective mechanism.

claim: The study reconstructs a complex and recent history of invasion by wild tomato onto the Galápagos Islands.
source: Our results reconstruct a complex and recent history of invasion by wild tomato onto the Galápagos Islands, and highlight the potential importance of gene flow during colonization.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The results highlight the potential importance of gene flow during colonization.
source: Our results reconstruct a complex and recent history of invasion by wild tomato onto the Galápagos Islands, and highlight the potential importance of gene flow during colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of introgression and phenotypic convergence.

claim: The finding of two separate molecular mechanisms underlying orange coloration each derived from CHS is highly suggestive that lighter fruit pigmentation is favored in the island environment.
source: While the adaptive benefit of orange fruits remains to be evaluated, our finding of two separate molecular mechanisms underlying orange coloration each derived from CHS is highly suggestive that lighter fruit pigmentation is favored in the island environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the repeated independent introgression of different carotenoid loci.

claim: This study underscores how admixture brought on by anthropogenic change can drive convergence over very short time scales.
source: Our results also add to an emerging phenotypic convergence literature by highlighting how admixture brought on by anthropogenic change can drive convergence over very short time scales.
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Leaf tissue was dried in silica and DNA was extracted using Qiagen Plant Mini Kits.
source: Leaf tissue was dried in silica and DNA was extracted using Qiagen Plant Mini Kits (Qiagen, Valencia, CA).
evidence: This describes the DNA extraction methodology.

claim: Two double-digest restriction site associated DNA sequencing libraries were prepared using PstI and EcoRI enzymes.
source: Two double-digest restriction site associated DNA sequencing (ddRAD) libraries were prepared using PstI and EcoRI enzymes by the Indiana University Center for Genomics and Bioinformatics.
evidence: This describes the library preparation methodology.

claim: Libraries were sequenced across two Illumina NextSeq flowcells (150 bp, paired-end, mid-output).
source: Libraries were sequenced across two Illumina NextSeq flowcells (150 bp, paired-end, mind-output).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology.

claim: Reads were mapped to the S. lycopersicum reference genome version SL3.0 using BWA.
source: Reads were mapped to the S. lycopersicum reference genome version SL3.0 using BWA (Li and Durbin, 2009).
evidence: This describes the read mapping methodology.

claim: Mapped reads were assembled and variants were called with the Stacks ref_map pipeline.
source: Mapped reads were assembled and variants were called with the Stacks ref_map pipeline.
evidence: This describes the variant calling methodology.

claim: There is little evidence for allele dropout or mapping bias in the dataset.
source: Lastly, we also evaluated our dataset for two possible sources of bias—the potential effects of allele dropout (ADO) on genotype calls (Cariou et al., 2016) and mapping bias arising from using a single reference genome—and confirmed that there is little evidence for either source in our dataset (Appendix 1, section S6).
evidence: This is based on evaluation of potential biases in the data.
